name: Yara Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what you do on an ordinary shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and still the new hand on a haul truck, which makes me laugh some mornings. I check the tyres and brakes, follow the loader's signal and carry rock from the cut to the crusher. My partner Laila works at the food warehouse, and our two children are grown and living elsewhere. I like the quiet attention driving takes, though reversing into a narrow bay still makes me ask for a second guide. I finished secondary school, came to the mine recently, and the pay is better than anything I've earned before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the truck still needs someone listening to its brakes and watching the loader. I'd tell my friends the little screen shortcuts are useful, but nobody has changed our shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my newness matters more than the software if the foreman has to choose whom to keep. My six-month cushion helps, though I don't want to spend it learning a job twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep taking the haul-truck shifts and ask the senior driver to watch my reversing at the crusher. Put part of each pay packet into our savings while Laila's warehouse hours stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm relieved that the job I only just learned would remain a job. I still feel a little foolish when an experienced driver makes the same turn in one clean move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the foreman give you room to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. Last Tuesday I misjudged a bay and Omar, the senior driver, talked me back rather than taking the keys. I'm grateful, but I remember how quickly a queue of trucks forms behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is good; what does it make possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We finally cleared a repair bill on our flat. Now I put money aside every pay day instead of helping our grown children with every small expense. They're earning for themselves, though we still want to be there in an emergency.

think: I think my **newness** matters more than the software if the foreman has to choose whom to keep.
My six-month **cushion** helps, though I don't want to spend it learning a job twice.
do: Keep taking the **haul-truck shifts** and ask the senior driver to watch my reversing at the crusher.

feel: **Relieved**, with a little embarrassment that the familiar work still takes me longer than the old hands.

fieldNote: She focuses on her **junior standing** more than AI because she is still learning the haul truck.
Her **savings** and Laila's warehouse wages make a small technological change feel manageable, although she keeps practicing difficult manoeuvres.

steps.text: Keep driving haul trucks and practise reversing at the crusher
Add part of each mine pay packet to household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the dispatch screens may get smarter before a robot can handle our rough haul roads. I'd ask our union representative to get training and transfer rules in writing while workers can still bargain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI on my phone every day, but that doesn't qualify me to repair a truck or run a control room. I suspect the mine could trim dispatch and then quietly expect drivers to handle more paperwork between loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the mine's new dispatch display with Omar if management brings one in. Attend the next union meeting and ask which paid courses lead to actual mine vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious enough to try the new display. I feel uneasy about the dispatch colleagues because I know a useful screen can also become a reason to leave a vacancy empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the mine changes first for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch office sends us routes and keeps the load sheets. If software takes more of that checking, there may be fewer people in that room before the trucks drive themselves. The ramp still needs a pair of eyes for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a leaflet alone. I'd ask the union which course is paid and which opening it actually leads to. I can take some risk, but I won't buy a certificate that the mine doesn't recognise.

I'd ask our **union representative** to get training and transfer rules in writing while workers can still bargain.

I suspect the mine could **trim dispatch** and then quietly expect drivers to handle more paperwork between loads.

Attend the next **union meeting** and ask which paid courses lead to actual mine vacancies.
feel: **Curious** about the screen, but uneasy when I picture fewer colleagues at the start of a shift.
S1.quote: I use AI on my phone every day, but that doesn't qualify me to repair a truck or run a control room.
fieldNote: Her daily **AI use** makes a new dispatch display approachable, but she separates that from formal technical skill.
She expects **desk roles** to contract first and wants union information on real vacancies before committing her savings to study.

steps.text: Practise on a new dispatch display with senior driver Omar if introduced
Attend the next union meeting about paid mine courses and transfers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI in 2028 will first change planning and records; the truck still needs a driver until robots arrive around 2031. I'd push for a transfer agreement before the company starts counting three years as plenty of warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, I would still be the least seasoned driver, and a robot truck in 2031 could end this late start. Our savings buy time, but I can't assume retirement at 63 will pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the union this month for the mine's transfer rules and any paid equipment-maintenance places. Apply for an equipment trainee opening at another local mine if ours announces driver cuts after robot trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That short runway frightens me because I only just found this wage. I can think clearly enough to ask about transfers, but I wouldn't sleep easily once driver cuts were announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home when you tell Laila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the dates on the kitchen calendar: 2028 for the office, about 2031 for the driving. Laila would ask whether I can still get warehouse work if the mine goes. I'd say I don't know; I'd rather apply for mine training before that becomes the choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would a different mine take a trainee your age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might not, and I know that. There are several mines within a bus ride, so I'd at least ask about a paid trainee opening. I wouldn't quit a well-paid driving shift on the strength of a promise.

say: I'd say **AGI in 2028** will first change planning and records; the truck still needs a driver until robots arrive around 2031.
I'd push for a **transfer agreement** before the company starts counting three years as plenty of warning.
think: At **60**, I would still be the least seasoned driver, and a robot truck in 2031 could end this late start.
Our savings buy time, but I can't assume **retirement** at 63 will pay the bills.
do: Ask the **union** this month for the mine's transfer rules and any paid equipment-maintenance places.
Apply for an **equipment trainee** opening at another local mine if ours announces driver cuts after robot trials.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway, although having savings keeps me from feeling trapped.
S2.quote: Our savings buy time, but I can't assume retirement at 63 will pay the bills.
fieldNote: She expects **thinking work** to change in 2028 and robot driving to threaten her own income around 2031.
Her savings prevent immediate crisis, but **junior standing** at age 60 makes her doubt the mine will protect her place.

steps.text: Ask the union for written transfer rules and paid equipment-maintenance places
Apply for equipment trainee openings at another local mine if driver cuts begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2031 gives us time to bargain over retraining, with hands-on robots due around 2034. I'd say drivers shouldn't have to fund the mine's change out of their own pockets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when AGI arrives, I might still want paid shifts; our savings don't tell me what retirement income will be. By 2034, I'd be 66 and could lose the truck before I choose to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Request a paid maintenance course from the mine in 2027 and enrol if it offers a place. Keep my truck shifts while checking each year whether Laila and I can meet ordinary bills without mine wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to the thinking change gives me room to learn. The driving date still bothers me because I'd be 66 and might not be ready to leave paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course have to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want actual time with the hydraulic lines and the people who service these trucks, not just a video. Omar can show me what a hot bearing sounds like, but a recognised course would help me apply elsewhere. I'd take it if the mine paid for the place and kept my wage during it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you decide to stop driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laila and I would add up our household bills every year. Our grown children aren't schoolchildren with costs on our books, but repairs and food still cost money. I won't set a retirement date from the robot date alone.

say: I'd tell the crew **2031** gives us time to bargain over retraining, with hands-on robots due around 2034.
I'd say drivers shouldn't have to **fund** the mine's change out of their own pockets.
think: At **63** when AGI arrives, I might still want paid shifts; our savings don't tell me what retirement income will be.
By **2034**, I'd be 66 and could lose the truck before I choose to stop working.
do: Request a **paid maintenance course** from the mine in 2027 and enrol if it offers a place.
Keep my **truck shifts** while checking each year whether Laila and I can meet ordinary bills without mine wages.
feel: **Wary**, yet steadier because I could practise another job before the truck is replaced.
S3.quote: By 2034, I'd be 66 and could lose the truck before I choose to stop working.
fieldNote: She uses the longer warning to seek **funded training**, while keeping paid driving work during the transition.
The gap between **63 and 66** matters because she has not established that household savings can replace mine wages.

steps.text: Enrol in a mine-funded maintenance course if a paid place opens
Keep paid haul-truck shifts while checking household bills annually

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to ask for honest figures on jobs, with robot driving expected around 2039. I'd tell younger drivers the union should negotiate a path for them, not just an exit for older people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 when AGI arrives and 71 when robots follow, I may already have stopped driving, but I can't promise that today. I worry more about younger workers who would have decades of wages to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Review our retirement budget with Laila this winter and once each year after that. Bring a younger driver to the union meeting when transfer plans come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture choosing my own leaving date in this version. I'm still uneasy for the younger drivers and for the possibility that our savings won't stretch as far as we expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay until 71 if the work remained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if my health and the money pointed that way. My mother worked long past the age she expected because the roof needed replacing. I won't claim to know what we'll need in thirteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a younger driver ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named training place, paid time to take it, and a rule for who gets the next job. I'd take one of the newer drivers to the meeting so it isn't just my generation speaking. They have much more work ahead of them than I do.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough to ask for honest figures on jobs, with robot driving expected around 2039.
I'd tell younger drivers the **union** should negotiate a path for them, not just an exit for older people.
think: At **68** when AGI arrives and 71 when robots follow, I may already have stopped driving, but I can't promise that today.
I worry more about **younger workers** who would have decades of wages to replace.
do: Review our **retirement budget** with Laila this winter and once each year after that.
Bring a **younger driver** to the union meeting when transfer plans come up.
feel: **Cautiously hopeful** because I have years to make a choice with numbers rather than a guess.
S4.quote: At 68 when AGI arrives and 71 when robots follow, I may already have stopped driving, but I can't promise that today.
fieldNote: She treats the long warning as a chance to test **retirement finances** rather than assume she can leave work.
Her concern shifts towards **younger drivers**, whose working lives extend far beyond the expected robot date.

steps.text: Review household retirement budget with partner Laila each winter
Bring a younger driver to the union meeting on transfer plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. At 60 I would barely have found my feet in this truck, and the robots could take driving three years later. A paid equipment course and a written union agreement on transfers would help more than cheerful speeches. A mine can replace my truck before I have learned every sound it makes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether Laila wants me to keep taking a risk at the mine. She likes that I enjoy the work, but she wants the two of us to choose together if the job stops being worth it. Our children have their own lives; this decision is ours.

headlineQuote: A mine can replace my truck before I have learned every sound it makes.
portrait: At **58**, Yara is a new haul-truck miner learning the work on higher pay than she has previously earned.
Her partner works at a **food warehouse**, their children are grown, and their savings cover over six months.
She uses **AI daily** for small questions but puts safety judgments with experienced people beside the machine.
She favours a **union voice** and sees nearby mines as possible employers if her own mine cuts drivers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robot trucks could arrive in 2031 before she has established herself.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid equipment course** and a clear union agreement on transfers would give her a practical route through the change.
